judgments.reasoning_cat1: A statutory disclosure notice that recites the TRIA definition of terrorism verbatim; it is descriptive rather than operative, and its terms are fixed by federal certification rather than by construction.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It says the policy 'makes available' terrorism insurance, which sits somewhat oddly with the $-0- terrorism premium in c005 and the war/insurrection exclusion at c093, but a notice form is unlikely to be pitted against the operative Crime exclusions.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A plain recital of the federal reimbursement formula with a single fixed percentage; nothing in the wording admits two readings.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Nothing in the Crime Coverage Section or General Terms addresses federal reimbursement, so there is no provision for it to collide with.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A numeric cap statement; the only blemish is the OCR run-together 'ina Program Year', which does not change meaning.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It duplicates c004 in substance but the two are consistent (Treasury cap vs insurer cap), so no genuine internal inconsistency.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Definite terms — an aggregate threshold, a deductible condition and pro rata allocation by Treasury procedures; no term needs construing.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It restates c003 from the insurer's side and does not touch the Crime limits of liability in c116, so the fit is clean.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A single blank-filled figure of $-0-; it states a fact rather than a right and carries no ambiguous term.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: A zero terrorism premium is in mild tension with c001's statement that the policy 'makes available' terrorism insurance, but the premium bill and the notice are both non-operative.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: An informational statement about producer compensation with a website and phone number; it creates no obligation to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: No other provision of the policy addresses producer compensation, so there is nothing to reconcile it against.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A notice identifying which coverage sections are claims-made; the sentence is clear on its face.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It describes Executive Liability, EPL and Fiduciary coverage sections that Item 3 of the Declarations does not list as purchased (only General Terms, Crime and Special Coverage), a mismatch between the notice and the Coverage Summary.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A conditional statement about retroactive dates; 'if a claims-made coverage section contains' is expressly contingent and unambiguous.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: No coverage section in this policy contains a retroactive date and none of the named claims-made sections was purchased, so the clause is orphaned but not contradicted.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Standard claims-made explanatory language; 'claims actually made or incidents reported' is a familiar formulation with no live ambiguity here.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Crime Coverage Section is a discovery-based, not claims-made, cover, so this notice pulls against Crime Exclusion 19 (c110/c134) and Subsection 25 (c116/c130) if read as applying to it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Detailed and specific about the 60-day automatic and one-year optional extended reporting periods; the terms are numerically fixed.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It grants extended reporting rights only for coverage sections not purchased under this policy, and the Crime section instead uses a 60-day post-termination discovery window in c110 — parallel but different mechanisms.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A commercial explanation of claims-made rate maturity; it confers no rights and uses no operative term.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Nothing else in the instrument addresses premium maturity, so there is no provision to check it against.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: An all-caps Declarations warning; the quoted terms are all defined elsewhere and the sentence structure is standard.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It warns that limits will be eroded by 'DEFENSE COSTS' and that retentions apply, but the Crime section has no Defense Costs concept and c057 expressly says no retention applies to Investigative Expenses — a mismatch with the purchased coverage.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A boilerplate consideration recital subject to the rest of the policy; nothing in it is capable of two readings.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It defers to the Declarations and all other terms, and c015 supplies the priority rule, so it cannot itself conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Six words — 'Coverage shall extend anywhere in the world' — absolute on its face, but very short absolutes of this kind are exactly what parties fight about at the margins.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is expressly cut back by the trade sanctions endorsement c045 and is in tension with definitions keyed to US chartering (c069 Executive) and US/Canadian currency (c078), though c015 gives coverage-section terms priority.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The words 'inconsistent or in conflict' are the operative trigger and are not self-defining, but the priority rule itself is stated plainly.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: This is the instrument's own conflict-resolution rule, so it is the provision a court would reach for when reconciling the General Terms notice clause c021 with Crime Subsection 27 (c118) or the endorsements — a role that makes it a candidate for construction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A pure cross-reference definition; the term simply takes the meaning given in the applicable coverage section.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Crime Coverage Section contains no definition of 'Claim' at all, yet c021 and Endorsement 1 (c039-c043) impose Claim-notice machinery — leaving 'Claim' undefined for the only purchased liability cover.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-line referral definition with no ambiguous term of its own.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Crime Subsection 11 does define Insured (c074), so the referral resolves cleanly for this coverage section.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Identifies the Parent Organization by pointing to a specific Declarations item; entirely determinate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Item 1 names MEDIDATA SOLUTIONS INC. consistently in both Declarations, while Item 4 of the Crime Declarations spells it 'Medidate Solutions, Inc.', a discrepancy that touches c080 more than this clause.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Defines the period by reference to Item 2 and adds a proportionality rule for short or long periods; both limbs are specific.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Item 2 as printed reads 'To 42:01 A.M.' — an obvious typographic corruption of 12:01 — and Endorsement 3 (c130) changes what must occur 'during the Policy Period' from sustaining loss to discovering it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: States separateness of limits and retentions in plain terms, twice qualified by 'unless stated to the contrary'; nothing needs construing.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is consistent with Crime Subsection 25 (c116) and the per-Insuring-Clause limits in the Crime Declarations.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Long but concrete — designated addresses, effective dates on receipt, and an excuse for late notice where 'not reasonably possible', a standard and workable formula.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its general late-notice safe harbour sits alongside the different regime in Endorsement 1 (c039-c041, prejudice-based) and the strict condition precedent with 90-day and six-month deadlines in Crime Subsection 27 (c118), which c015 says would control.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Names a specific publication and three specific trigger dates for conversion; the mechanics are determinate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Crime Subsection 28 (c119) sets its own foreign currency rule keyed to the date of Discovery, which differs from this clause's judgment/settlement/loss-due triggers, though the opening 'Except as otherwise provided' harmonises them.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A conventional subrogation and cooperation clause; 'everything necessary' is broad but is a familiar and workable standard.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It reads consistently with the Recoveries waterfall in c120, which allocates recoveries after payment rather than contradicting subrogation.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Full compliance with all the terms of this policy' as a condition precedent is a sweeping, one-sided formulation whose reach against a minor breach is genuinely contestable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is hard to square with c021's and Endorsement 1's express rules that a late notice does not invalidate coverage absent prejudice, and with the two-year suit limitation in c118.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: An enumerated agency list with one express carve-out; the enumeration is closed and specific.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The exception for 'giving of notice to apply for an Extended Reporting Period' refers to a mechanism the purchased Crime section does not contain, a small orphan reference.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: An exclusive-formalities clause naming the required signatory; definite and easily applied.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The endorsements are signed only by an 'Authorized Representative' with an illegible mark, which is at least arguably short of 'an authorized employee of Chubb & Son' — but no party disputed endorsement validity.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A specific 20-day notice rule for the first 60 days, driven by New York statute; the numbers leave nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It fits the structure of the rest of Subsection 11 and the notice-copy requirement in c034.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: An enumerated list of statutory termination grounds; item (iv) turns on 'substantially and materially increases the hazard', a genuinely elastic standard, and (v) on 'material change in the nature or extent of the risk'.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The grounds are exhaustive and consistent with c027 and c035's requirement that the notice state the specific reason.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short and mechanical rule for insured-initiated termination keyed to written notice before the effective date.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It dovetails with the short-rate refund rule in c032, which expressly addresses termination by the Parent Organization.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'At such other time as may be agreed upon' is open-ended by design; mutual agreement supplies the content.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is the residual limb of an otherwise closed list and does not undercut any other termination mechanism.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Expiration and nonrenewal keyed to Item 2 with an express cross-reference to paragraph (g); definite.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The cross-reference to paragraph (g) is accurate and paragraph (g) (c033) delivers the promised notice machinery.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Customary short rates' is an undefined trade term whose computation is not spelled out anywhere in the policy.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is consistent with the termination grid in c027-c031 and nothing else in the instrument sets a refund basis.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Long but almost entirely numeric — 60/120 days, 10% of expiring rate, 30-day and 60-day sub-rules — and each contingency is separately addressed.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Sub-paragraph (iii) increases aggregate limits pro rata for extensions, which interacts with but does not contradict the Policy Period proportionality rule in c019.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A single mechanical obligation to copy the broker at its last known address; nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is consistent with the notice obligations elsewhere in Subsection 11.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Requires the notice to state specific reasons and an effective date; short and determinate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: In the source text this sub-paragraph runs directly into the heading of Subsection 12, an OCR/formatting merger, but the substantive fit with c027-c033 is clean.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Terminates prior bonds identified in Item 4 as of inception; the reference is specific and self-executing.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It overlaps with the last paragraph of Crime Subsection 24 (c115), which Endorsement 3 (c129) deletes in its entirety — leaving this General Terms provision as the only surviving prior-bond termination rule.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-sentence bankruptcy clause preserving the insurer's rights and obligations; standard and clear.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Nothing elsewhere addresses insured insolvency, so there is no counterpart to conflict with.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A headings-are-not-substantive clause; about as determinate as drafting gets.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is repeated in each endorsement (c044, c046, c123, c126, c131, c133, c135) consistently, so no incoherence arises.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Has prejudiced the Company' is the operative trigger and is an inherently fact-laden standard, but it is the statutory New York formula and is qualified expressly by paragraph (2).
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It relaxes the notice consequences that c021 and the condition-precedent language of Crime Subsection 27 (c118) impose, and c024 still says no action lies without 'full compliance with all the terms' — a real pull in opposite directions.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Not reasonably possible' and 'as soon as reasonably possible' are elastic, but they are settled statutory phrases and mirror the same words in c021.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It duplicates the last paragraph of c021 almost word for word, so the two are consistent rather than in conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A clean two-year burden-shifting rule with an irrebuttable presumption; the categories are specific and the numbers fixed.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The endorsement's paragraph numbering is scrambled in the text (the '(1) (2) (3) (4)' block appears together in c039), so which paragraph 'the above paragraph' refers to is not obvious on the face of the assembled document.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A narrow saving clause preserving claims-made timing and barring duplicate coverage; specific in what it preserves.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It preserves 'claims made during the Policy Period' rules that exist only in unpurchased coverage sections, so it has little to operate on in a Crime-only policy.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Death or personal injury, as that term is defined by the New York Insurance Law' anchors the key phrase to an external statute, but the direct-action right and 60-day carve-out are otherwise mechanical.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It says the injured person may sue 'notwithstanding any other provision', which flatly cuts across c024's bar on joining or impleading the Company in any action.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Boilerplate headings and 'all other terms remain unchanged'; nothing susceptible of two readings in isolation.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: 'All other terms shall remain unchanged' is the phrase that has to absorb the competing amendments to Exclusion 19 in c127 and c134, but that strain shows up in those clauses, not here.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'To the extent that trade or economic sanctions or other similar laws or regulations prohibit' is a general catch-all with no enumerated specifics to anchor it, and its reach is genuinely open.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It cuts back the unqualified worldwide grant in c014 without saying so, and c015's priority rule does not obviously resolve which prevails.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Identical headings boilerplate to c044; determinate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the corresponding clauses in every other endorsement.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A consideration recital subordinating the coverage section to the Declarations and General Terms; no operative ambiguity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It says the coverage section is subject to the General Terms while c015 says coverage-section terms control over inconsistent General Terms — a circularity, though the standard reading harmonises them.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Direct loss' is the load-bearing and undefined phrase, and 'in collusion with others' broadens the grant, but the clause is short and its elements are all defined terms.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It says loss 'sustained by an Insured' whereas the parallel clauses 2-8 say 'sustained by an Organization', and Ownership (c111) and Exclusion 13 (c104) both cut it back; c112 also rewrites it wholesale for ERISA Plans.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: An itemised premises grant with four enumerated sub-limbs; the closing 'committed by a Third Party' qualifier is oddly placed and its reach over sub-limbs (i)-(iv) is not obvious.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Exclusions 14 (c105) and 15 (c106) carve it back in specific and consistent ways, and it did not bear on the wire-transfer loss at issue.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Same structure as the premises clause with the same trailing 'committed by a Third Party' qualifier, plus 'temporarily within the home of an Employee or an Organization', which is odd applied to an entity.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It reads consistently with the In Transit definition (c075) and Exclusion 14 (c105), which excepts carriers for hire other than armored car companies.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The general grant — 'Forgery or alteration of a Financial Instrument' — is followed by an 'including' list of three very particular check scenarios, so the reach of the general words against the enumerated specifics is exactly the ejusdem generis / expressio unius problem; whether 'including' is illustrative or limiting is contestable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its operation depends entirely on the Financial Instrument definition (c070, limited to a check, draft or similar written promise to pay a sum certain) and the Forgery definition (c071), and it also has to be read with Exclusion 16 (c107) and the Legal Expenses Extension (c113).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A single sentence whose whole content is the undefined phrase 'direct loss' plus the defined terms Computer Fraud and Third Party; 'direct' and the causal 'resulting from' are the classic battlegrounds in computer-crime cover.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It cannot be applied without the chain of definitions in c060, c061, c062 and c065, and is cut back by Exclusion 15 (c106), Exclusion 12(k) (c100) and the privacy endorsement (c125), which preserves only Insuring Clause 6 — so a loss covered here could be excluded there.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Again a one-line grant turning on 'direct loss ... resulting from Funds Transfer Fraud committed by a Third Party'; the word 'direct' and the Third Party requirement are the points where two readings are plainly available.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It depends on the Funds Transfer Fraud definition's 'without such Organization's knowledge or consent' (c072), and the privacy endorsement (c125) singles this clause out for preservation, showing the drafters knew the exclusions otherwise bite on it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short grant referring to a tightly drawn defined term; 'direct loss' is the only elastic word and the underlying definition is narrow.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Exclusion 12(k) (c100) expressly preserves Insuring Clause 7, and Exclusion 14 (c105) excludes this peril from Clauses 2 and 3, so the architecture is coherent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-line grant depending on the Credit Card Fraud definition; nothing in the sentence itself carries two meanings.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Exclusion 18 (c109) excludes precisely the forgery of written instruments that the Credit Card Fraud definition (c064) makes the subject of coverage, restoring it only on two conditions — an unusually circular relationship.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Not in collusion with such Client's employees' is a specific and workable limit, and the rest is defined terms.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It fits with the Client definition (c059), the Ownership rule for Clause 9 in c111 and Exclusion 13 (c104), all of which point the same way.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Reasonable expenses' and 'prior written consent' are supplied by the definitions; the retention gating language, however, first requires loss in excess of the Retention and then says no Retention applies, which reads awkwardly.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The 'No Retention shall apply' sentence is in tension with the last paragraph of c116, which makes the Company liable only for loss in excess of the applicable Retention, and with Exclusion 12(g) (c096), which carves these expenses out of the consequential loss bar.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Or similar financial institution' is a general catch-all appended to two named specifics, leaving its outer boundary uncertain.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is used consistently in Insuring Clause 2 (c049) and sits alongside Exclusion 12(m) (c102), which excludes loss while in a bank's custody — a coverage/exclusion overlap worth noting.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'A customer ... to whom such Organization provides goods or services under written contract or for a fee' has two concrete alternative qualifiers; determinate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with Insuring Clause 9 (c056), the Ownership rule (c111) and the carve-outs excluding Client expenses in c063 and c076.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'The unlawful taking or the fraudulently induced transfer of Money ... resulting from a Computer Violation' packs two quite different concepts together, and whether a transfer induced by a spoofed communication is 'resulting from' a Computer Violation is genuinely open on these words.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is meaningless without Computer Violation (c062), Computer System (c061) and Data (c065), and Insuring Clause 5 (c052) plus Exclusion 15 (c106) and Exclusion 12(k) (c100) all pull on the same phrase.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The proviso 'owned and operated or leased and operated by an Organization' is the crux: whether a hosted third-party email service is within the insured's Computer System is not answerable from these words alone.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is the gateway to Computer Violation (c062) and thence Computer Fraud (c060) and Insuring Clause 5 (c052), and the Data definition (c065) circularly refers back to it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'The fraudulent ... entry of Data into ... a Computer System' and 'change to Data elements or program logic' are broad and undefined at the edges, and the trailing qualifier 'directed against an Organization' is of uncertain application to limbs (a)-(c).
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is the operative content of Computer Fraud (c060) and Computer Violation Expenses (c063), and its reach has to be squared with the privacy/data-breach exclusion in c125 which preserves only Insuring Clause 6.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Reasonable expenses' and 'substantially the same level of operational capability' are soft, but the definition is otherwise carefully bounded by consent and exclusion of Client costs.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It depends on Computer Violation (c062) and is expressly carved out of Exclusion 12(g) (c096) and limited by Exclusion 12(h) (c097), which fit together coherently.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Defines Credit Card Fraud by reference to Forgery of 'any written instrument required in connection with any credit card' — 'required in connection with' is broad and undefined.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Exclusion 18 (c109) then excludes loss caused by 'any forgery or alteration of, on or in any written instrument' under Insuring Clause 8, which on its face swallows the very coverage this definition creates unless the two conditions are met.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'A representation of information, knowledge, facts, concepts or instructions which are processed and stored in a Computer System' is a broad list-plus-qualifier, and whether an email or its header fields count is not settled by the words.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It feeds directly into Computer Violation (c062) and Computer System (c061), so any dispute about the reach of the computer-fraud cover runs through it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Facts which would cause a reasonable person to assume' is a deliberately elastic trigger, and the inclusive list of (a)-(c) plus the collusion carve-back adds further scope for argument.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Discovery is the pivot of Exclusion 19 in all three of its competing forms (c110, c127, c134), of the notice conditions in c118, and of the amended Subsection 25 in c130, so its meaning is entangled with an already inconsistent set.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A four-limbed definition with concrete tests (compensation by Salary, right to govern and direct); the boundary with independent contractors is drawn by Exclusion 13 rather than left open here.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Limb (c) folds Executive into Employee while Exclusion 12(c) (c092) separately excludes partner theft and Exclusion 13(a) (c104) excludes contractor-caused loss — overlapping but reconcilable.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Defined by reference to ERISA Title 1 and a specific operating structure; the external statute supplies the content.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It works with c067(d), c074 and the ERISA Plan provision c112, which are consistent with one another.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Equivalent positions of (a) or (b) above' in a foreign-chartered Organization is a general equivalence test appended to an enumerated list, whose boundary is genuinely uncertain.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Subparagraph (a) is replaced wholesale by Endorsement 1 (c122) to add 'trustee', so the version printed in the body is superseded and a reader of the base form alone would be misled.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'A check, draft or similar written promise, order or direction to pay a sum certain in Money' is a general phrase following two named specifics — the paradigm ejusdem generis question of whether an electronic instruction can be a 'similar written' direction.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It controls the scope of Insuring Clause 4 (c051) and the Legal Expenses Extension (c113), and it must be read against the Forgery definition (c071), which contemplates electronically produced signatures.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'The signing of the name of another natural person or organization, with the intent to deceive' followed by an exclusion for signatures including one's own name, and a deeming rule for electronic signatures, is a definition with several movable parts and a real question whether a spoofed sender name is a 'signing'.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It has to be reconciled with the Financial Instrument definition (c070) that gates Insuring Clause 4 (c051), with Credit Card Fraud (c064) and Exclusion 18 (c109), and with the 'other than Forgery' carve-out in the Funds Transfer Fraud definition (c072).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Fraudulent ... instructions ... purportedly issued by an Organization ... without such Organization's knowledge or consent' is internally awkward — instructions purportedly from the insured but sent without its consent — and 'knowledge or consent' invites two readings where an employee was deceived into authorising.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It expressly excepts Forgery (c071) and so must be read against Insuring Clause 4 (c051), and the privacy endorsement (c125) singles out Insuring Clause 6 for preservation.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Any Employee, including a risk manager, designated to represent an Insured' is short; 'designated' is unqualified as to how designation occurs.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It matters for Discovery (c066) and Exclusion 13(b) (c104), both of which turn on what an Insurance Representative knew, and the term is used consistently.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short definition with one Insuring-Clause-specific extension; 'Non-ERISA Pian' is an obvious OCR slip that does not alter meaning.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Insuring Clause 1 (c048) pays for loss sustained by an Insured while Clauses 2-8 say Organization, and c112 amends Clause 1 for ERISA Plans — the definitions are broader than some clauses assume.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Specifies the custodians and the exact start and end of conveyance; unusually precise for a coverage definition.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It matches Insuring Clause 3 (c050) and Exclusion 14(b) (c105), which addresses carriers for hire, without inconsistency.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Reasonable expenses ... to establish the existence and amount of a covered loss' with an express exclusion of internal costs and Client expenses; the only soft word is 'reasonable'.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It works with Insuring Clause 10 (c057) and the carve-out in Exclusion 12(g) (c096), all pointing the same way.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A four-item closed list — currency, coin, bank notes and bullion — with no catch-all.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Whether a wire-transferred balance is 'Money' as so defined is a question that arises when this definition is read with Insuring Clauses 5 and 6, but the definition itself is stable across the instrument.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Two specific limbs, each tightly drawn as to instrument type and currency; nothing general is left hanging.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Exclusion 12(k) (c100) expressly preserves Insuring Clause 7, so the coverage and exclusion structure is consistent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A mirror of the ERISA Plan definition keyed to plans not subject to Title 1; determinate by reference.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is picked up only by c074 for Insuring Clause 1, and c112's ERISA-specific amendments do not extend to Non-ERISA Plans — a gap rather than a conflict.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A pure pointer to Item 4 of the Declarations; the definition itself has no elastic term.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Item 4 as printed reads 'Medidate Solutions, Inc., and its subsidiaries' — a misspelling of the named insured and an undefined use of 'subsidiaries' alongside the defined term Subsidiary in c087 and the Changes in Exposure machinery in c114.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'The interior portion of a building occupied by an Organization in conducting its business' is short and concrete, though 'interior portion' and 'occupied' have edges.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is used consistently in Insuring Clauses 2 and 3, Safe Burglary (c084) and In Transit (c075), and the Ownership proviso in c111 addresses damage to Premises.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Tangible property other than Money or Securities' is a clean residual definition drawn against two other defined terms.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It fits the tripartite Money/Securities/Property scheme used throughout the insuring clauses and exclusions without slippage.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The parenthetical exception '(except a person acting as a watchman, porter or janitor)' is an enumerated carve-out inside a definition, and 'violence or threat of violence ... in the presence and cognizance of' is fact-specific but standard.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is used as the pivot in Insuring Clauses 2 and 3, in Exclusion 12(n) (c103) and in Exclusion 15 (c106), all consistently.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'By forcible or violent entry evidenced by visible marks' is an unusually concrete evidentiary requirement; little room for two readings.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It aligns with Insuring Clause 2(ii)-(iv), Exclusion 12(j)(ii) (c099) and Exclusion 12(n) (c103).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: An inclusive list ('including bonus, commission, incentive payments, and the cost of health, welfare and pension benefits') with no closing catch-all, so its outer edge is set by 'compensation'.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is used in the Employee definition (c067), in the internal-costs carve-outs (c063, c076) and in Exclusion 12(a) (c090), consistently in each.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The text reads 'negotiable and nor-negotiable', an evident mechanical corruption of 'non-negotiable', and 'contracts representing either Money or Property' is broad enough to invite argument.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Securities is a core term in every insuring clause and in the valuation rules of c119, so a defect in it propagates, but no other provision contradicts it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A precise majority-ownership test with 'directly or indirectly, in any combination' as the only broadening phrase.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is used in Changes in Exposure (c114, as amended by c128) and sits against Item 4's undefined lowercase 'subsidiaries' in the Declarations, referenced by c080.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Unlawful taking ... to the deprivation of' is compressed, and the definition is expressly split between Insuring Clauses 1 and 9 rather than left general.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It works with Insuring Clauses 1 and 9, Exclusion 12(c) (c092), Exclusion 12(n) (c103) and Exclusion 13 (c104), and c112 replaces 'Theft' with 'fraudulent or dishonest act' for ERISA Plan losses.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Defined negatively as a natural person who is not an Employee and not in collusion with one; the restriction to 'natural person' is a real limit whose application to an unidentified remote actor can be contested.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Every one of Insuring Clauses 2 through 8 requires a Third Party, so if the perpetrator cannot be shown to be a natural person the whole set of clauses is affected — a definition doing a great deal of load-bearing work.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Directly or indirectly' plus 'authorized or unauthorized' plus 'genuine or fictitious account' is deliberately maximal, and the proviso's definition of 'such loss' as only the improper financial gain is a narrowing that could be read several ways.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The proviso interacts with the Salary definition (c085) and with the indirect-loss exclusion (c096), and both use 'directly or indirectly' consistently.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Or other confidential information of any kind' is an unbounded catch-all following two specifics — a textbook general-versus-specific scope problem.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: This exclusion is deleted outright by Endorsement 2 (c124) and replaced by the broader privacy regime in c125, so the version printed in the body no longer operates — a trap for anyone reading the base form.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The exclusion is clear but the proviso's excess formula (partner's percentage ownership multiplied by total assets 'as reflected in the most recent audited financial statements') is intricate and could be computed more than one way.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It presupposes a partnership structure while the named insured is a corporation, and it interacts with the 'partner' limb of the Executive definition (c069) and Employee (c067).

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A long enumerated list closing with 'or any act or condition incident to any of the foregoing' — a general catch-all whose reach against the specifics is the classic ejusdem generis question, and 'governmental intervention' is itself broad.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits uneasily with the terrorism disclosure notice (c001) stating that the policy makes terrorism coverage available, since acts of terrorism could readily be argued into 'usurped power' or 'insurrection'.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Three named nuclear perils plus the same 'any act or condition incident to any of the foregoing' catch-all, though the specifics here are narrower and better understood.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: No other provision addresses nuclear risk, so there is nothing to reconcile it against.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Loss of income not realized as the result of a covered loss' is a compressed double negative whose scope — lost profits only, or any unearned income — is not obvious from the words.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It overlaps substantially with the indirect and consequential loss exclusion in c096, and neither says which governs where both could apply.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Indirect or consequential loss or damage of any kind' is about as general as an exclusion gets, and its interaction with the undefined 'direct loss' in every insuring clause is a live definitional question.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It expressly excepts Investigative and Computer Violation Expenses under Insuring Clause 10 (c057), and it overlaps with the loss-of-income exclusion c095; read with the 'direct loss' requirement in c052 and c053 it is the exclusion most likely to be pressed against a computer-fraud claim.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Four itemised sub-limbs, each narrowly drawn (illegal copies, replacement equipment, design or improvement, magnetic media), with no residual catch-all.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It carves back the Computer Violation Expenses coverage in c057 and c063 in ways that are specific and do not swallow it.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A short exclusion of litigation costs with an express proviso preserving Subsection 22; the cross-reference is precise.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Subsection 22 (c113) does exist and grants exactly the costs preserved, so the cross-reference works; the two-year suit bar in c118 also references Subsection 22 consistently.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The sub-paragraph is mislabelled '(i)' where it should read '(j)' while its own proviso calls itself 'Exclusion 12(j)' — a mechanical labelling error inside the clause.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The mislabelling collides with the genuine Exclusion 12(i) at c098, so a reader tracing a cross-reference to '12(i)' cannot tell which is meant.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Knowingly having given or surrendered ... in any exchange or purchase' is broad and the proviso restores only Insuring Clause 7 and Property loss under Clause 5, an asymmetry that begs the question why Money under Clause 5 is treated differently.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: That asymmetry bears directly on Insuring Clause 5 (c052), whose grant covers Money, Securities or Property, and on the fraudulently-induced-transfer limb of the Computer Fraud definition (c060) — a voluntary-transfer exclusion against an induced-transfer coverage.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Eight words — 'loss sustained by one Insured to the advantage of any other Insured' — with 'to the advantage of' entirely undefined and capable of narrow or sweeping application.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: With multiple Insureds (Organization plus ERISA and Non-ERISA Plans under c074) and the non-accumulation rule in c117, the exclusion's reach across affiliated entities is not obviously bounded.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Similar recognized place of safe deposit' and 'any person who is duly authorized ... to have custody' are broad general phrases sitting after named specifics, and the excess proviso is intricate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its 'any person duly authorized to have custody' language would on its face exclude much of what Insuring Clause 3 (c050) and the In Transit definition (c075) expressly cover, and it duplicates the Other Insurance clause c121.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Other fraudulent, dishonest or criminal act' is a catch-all closing a list of named perils, and 'any authorized representative of an Insured' is used without being a defined term anywhere in the policy.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: 'Authorized representative' also appears nowhere else in the Crime section, while Exclusion 13(a) (c104) uses a different formula ('other similar representative'), so the two exclusions overlap without either defining the class.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Limb (a) ends with 'or other similar representative' after a list of eight agent types — the paradigm ejusdem generis problem — and limb (b) turns on when an Executive 'becomes aware', an inherently contestable point.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The awareness trigger overlaps with but is not identical to the Discovery definition in c066, and 'other similar representative' overlaps with 'any authorized representative' in Exclusion 12(n) (c103) without either being reconciled.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Two limbs, each listing named perils and a specific custody scenario with an armored-car exception; nothing general is left dangling.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It coordinates cleanly with Insuring Clauses 2 and 3 (c049, c050) and with Exclusion 12(m) (c102), which also carves out armored motor vehicle companies.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: '(as distinct from Robbery)' is an express contrast that helps, but 'kidnap, ransom or other extortion payment ... surrendered to any person as a result of a threat' is a wide formulation whose edge against a fraudulently induced transfer is arguable.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The Schedule of Forms lists a Kidnap/Ransom & Extortion Coverage Section that the Declarations Item 3 does not include, so this exclusion points at a cover the assembled policy does not contain.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Confined to registered or coupon obligations and coupons 'whether attached or detached'; specific and self-limiting.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It narrows Insuring Clause 4 (c051) in a way consistent with the Financial Instrument definition (c070), which is itself limited to checks, drafts and similar written directions.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'After an Organization becomes aware' is a softer and different trigger from the policy's defined Discovery, and 'other fraudulent, dishonest or criminal act' is a catch-all after a named peril.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: This exclusion is deleted outright by Endorsement 4 (c132), so the text printed in the body no longer operates — a direct contradiction between body and endorsement for anyone reading the form.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It excludes 'loss caused by any forgery or alteration of, on or in any written instrument' — the very thing Credit Card Fraud is defined as — and then restores it on two conditions, a circular structure inviting argument about what is left.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Read against the Credit Card Fraud definition (c064) and Insuring Clause 8 (c055), the exclusion appears to swallow the grant unless the proviso is treated as the real coverage condition.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Limbs (a), (b) and (c) are near-identical and largely redundant, and it is not clear whether the sixty-day window governs only the notice or also the Discovery — an ambiguity in a clause that can defeat coverage entirely.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Exclusion 19 is amended 'in its entirety' twice, by Endorsement 3 (c127) and again by Endorsement 5 (c134), with materially different texts, so three versions of the same numbered exclusion coexist; c112(b) also purports to substitute 'one (1) year' for words the c127 version does not contain.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Owned by ... or for which the Organization is legally liable, or held ... in any capacity whether or not the Organization is liable' is broad but the three limbs are cumulative and the two provisos are specific.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It sits with Insuring Clause 1 (c048), which speaks of loss sustained by an Insured rather than an Organization, and with the Client coverage in c056, and the ERISA amendment in c112 changes who sustains the loss again.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It amends Insuring Clause 1 to cover a 'fraudulent or dishonest act' — a broader and undefined phrase replacing the defined Theft or Forgery — and directs a mechanical word substitution in another provision.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its instruction to delete 'sixty (60) days' from Exclusion 19 cannot be carried out on the Endorsement 3 version of Exclusion 19 (c127), which contains no such words, and the retention waiver here pulls against the retention rule in c116.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Reasonable court costs and attorneys' fees' with prior written consent, tied to two specified Insuring Clauses; the boundaries are drawn by cross-reference rather than left open.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It is expressly preserved by Exclusion 12(i) (c098) and picked up by the special limitation period in c118(b), and it says the payment is 'in addition to' the Limits, which sits alongside c116's caps without contradicting them.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The automatic-coverage grant and the 10%-of-revenues notice condition are numerically specific, though 'as soon as practicable' and the Company's 'sole discretion' to impose different terms are open-ended.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its first paragraph is replaced by Endorsement 3 (c128), which changes the grant from coverage 'after the effective date' to coverage for loss 'Discovered after' that date, so the body text as printed is superseded.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A four-condition prior-loss regime plus a maximum-liability rule; each condition is concrete and the anti-stacking language is explicit.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Endorsement 3 (c129) deletes Subsection 24 in its entirety and directs that all references to it be deleted, so this provision is wholly displaced while c116 still opens with 'Subject to Subsection 24'.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Very long but almost entirely mechanical; the softer parts are 'any series of related acts, casualties or events' and 'concerned or implicated', which are the usual aggregation battlegrounds.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its opening words 'Subject to Subsection 24' point to a subsection Endorsement 3 deletes (c129), and its first paragraph is itself replaced by c130 with a different trigger (sustained before termination and Discovered during the Policy Period), leaving the printed and amended texts inconsistent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Two short anti-stacking sentences; the only oddity is the OCR 'fo any loss', which does not change meaning.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It reinforces c116's single-limit rule and the anti-stacking language in c115, so the three point the same way.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'At the earliest practicable moment' is a vague standard bolted onto hard 90-day and six-month outer limits, and the inventory-comparison proviso is convoluted; the two-year suit bar runs from 'any Discovery', which is itself an elastic trigger.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Making these steps a condition precedent is hard to reconcile with c021's excuse for impossible-to-give notice and with Endorsement 1 (c039), which says late notice does not invalidate coverage absent prejudice, and the 60-day windows in Exclusion 19 (c110/c134) run on a different clock.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A detailed least-of valuation table keyed to named publications and specific dates; 'actual cash value' is the only conventional soft term.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It differs from the General Terms currency rule in c022, but c022 opens with 'Except as otherwise provided in any coverage section' and c015 gives this section priority, so the conflict is expressly resolved.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A four-step waterfall with fixed priorities and an express exclusion of reinsurance recoveries; nothing needs construing.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It coexists with the General Terms subrogation clause c023 without contradiction, since that clause creates the right and this one allocates the proceeds.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Null and void to the extent of the amount recoverable or received' is a strong formulation, and 'recoverable' as against 'received' is a real distinction that can decide a case.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It substantially duplicates the excess proviso in Exclusion 12(m) (c102), and 'null and void' sits awkwardly with the excess-cover proviso in its own second half.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A precise substitution of one word ('trustee') into a specified subparagraph; there is nothing else to read.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It amends only subparagraph (a) of Executive (c069), leaving (b)-(d) in place, which is coherent.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Standard headings and unchanged-terms boilerplate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the identical clauses in every other endorsement and with c038.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-line deletion identifying the exclusion by number; entirely determinate on its face.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It removes Exclusion 12(b) (c091) while c125 substitutes a broader privacy regime, so a reader of the body text alone would apply an exclusion that no longer exists.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Each limb closes with 'or any similar type of nonpublic information' after a long enumeration, and 'loss involving the ... use of' confidential information is extraordinarily broad — a general-versus-specific and vagueness problem at once.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Its carve-out preserves only Insuring Clause 6, which implies it does bite on Insuring Clause 5 (c052) even though a computer fraud will almost always 'involve the use of' the insured's information — a serious pull against the computer fraud grant.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Headings and unchanged-terms boilerplate; determinate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the corresponding clauses in the other endorsements.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: The three limbs are again largely redundant, and the endorsement removes the notice requirement entirely so that discovery alone matters — a substantive change whose intended interaction with the notice conditions elsewhere is not stated.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It amends Exclusion 19 'in its entirety' but Endorsement 5 (c134) does the same thing with different text restoring the sixty-day notice, and c112(b) directs a substitution of words this version does not contain.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A replacement first paragraph changing the coverage trigger to loss 'Discovered after the effective date' of the acquisition; the change is expressed plainly.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It leaves the second paragraph of Subsection 23 (c114) — with its 10% revenue test and sixty-day notice — in place around a differently triggered first paragraph, and its Discovery-based trigger has to be squared with the amended Subsection 25 in c130.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: 'Any and all references to Subsection 24 are deleted in their entirety' is a sweeping instruction whose effect on the opening words of other provisions must be worked out by the reader.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Subsection 25 (c116) opens 'Subject to Subsection 24 Liability for Prior Losses', and although c130 replaces that first paragraph, this deletion instruction and c115 together create a document in which a deleted subsection is still referenced on the page.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: One replacement sentence — liability only for loss sustained before termination and Discovered during the Policy Period — which is clear but reverses the temporal test in the text it replaces.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It conflicts with the body of Subsection 25 (c116), which says the Company is liable for loss sustained during the Policy Period, and with the sixty-day post-termination discovery window that Endorsement 5 (c134) restores to Exclusion 19.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Headings boilerplate plus 'all other terms ... shall remain unchanged'; nothing ambiguous in itself.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The 'remain unchanged' formula is precisely what has to reconcile this endorsement's rewrite of Exclusion 19 with Endorsement 5's competing rewrite (c134), but the strain lies in those clauses.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: A one-line deletion identified by exclusion number; there is nothing to construe.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It removes Exclusion 17 (c108) from the body of the coverage section, so the printed text and the endorsed policy differ — a coordination point rather than a contradiction.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Headings and unchanged-terms boilerplate.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: Consistent with the equivalent clauses in the other endorsements.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: It repeats the three redundant limbs and the ambiguity over whether the sixty days governs Discovery as well as notice, and adds a new limitation to renewals 'issued by the Company or by any affiliate' that the body version lacks.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: It amends Exclusion 19 'in its entirety' after Endorsement 3 (c127) has already done so with materially different text; both bear the same effective date, so which controls is genuinely open, and c112(b)'s substitution instruction only fits this version.

judgments.reasoning_cat1: Headings boilerplate with a page-break artifact embedded; the substance is standard.
judgments.reasoning_cat2: The 'all other terms remain unchanged' formula here is the same one appearing in c131, and the two endorsements it belongs to amend the same exclusion differently.
